title: Nia and the Stream Light
markdown:
Moonlight, soft as warm milk, spilled into Nia’s room. Wisp the kitty was already a sleepy curve on the sill. Nia and Dr. Sol, a wise old owl with little spectacles, were getting ready for stargazing, their favourite time.

“Oh, Wisp,” Nia whispered, voice like falling snow. “It’s so peaceful. I wish our star chart lamp glowed a little brighter. Hard to see the faraway stars when the light is dim.”

Dr. Sol hooted gently. “A bit more gentle light would help. A soft steady glow for the clubhouse.”

Nia tapped her chin. “Like the big lights in town?”

Wisp blinked green eyes, a silent question.

“Look outside,” Dr. Sol whispered. “What moves with a gentle, steady rhythm all day long?”

Nia peeked. “The sunshine! So strong. I wish we could catch some for our lamp.”

“Sunshine is wonderful, but it rests when the stars wake. What else moves?”

A breeze made the willow leaves dance. “The wind! It makes the leaves whisper.”

“The wind can turn windmills. Sometimes it is only a whisper, too soft for our lamp.”

Wisp yawned, pink tongue, tail a slow sleepy swish.

“And the little stream that murmurs past the garden? The one that always, always flows?”

Nia’s eyes widened. “The water. Always moving, always downstream. Such a steady rhythm.”

“Precisely.”

Nia pictured a tiny wooden wheel in the stream, water nudging it, turning it, a tiny bit of power for the lamp.

“So the water’s steady movement could make our lamp glow?”

“It could. Sun is lovely. Wind is exciting. The gentle flow can give us power even when sun and wind are resting. Reliable light.”

They tiptoed to the stream. Nia found a sturdy twig. Dr. Sol helped with a strong maple leaf and a smooth round pebble. Carefully they fashioned a tiny wheel and set it where the water ran most steadily. Soft plink. The water nudged the leaf-wheel. It turned, its quiet whisper blending with the stream’s song.

Back in the clubhouse they connected the wheel to the lamp — a fable-sized join, a mechanic’s hope scaled to owl and child. A tiny bulb flickered, then held a soft steady glow. Painted constellations on the ceiling shimmered. Wisp curled close, purrs a soft rumble.

“We made power from the stream.”

Dr. Sol nodded. He did not list the world’s energies as a bedtime exam. The lamp hummed, a quiet lullaby of moving water. Nia yawned. Wisp’s purrs slowed. The faraway stars, at last, were easier to point at, and the stream, which had not been asked to rest, kept turning the little wheel as if that had always been part of its job.
